text: With the sale under two weeks out, Theo runs a k6 load test against checkout-api's real endpoint, ramping virtual users from zero to 500 and checking real thresholds: p95 latency under 300 milliseconds, error rate under 1 percent. It's a genuinely reasonable test design.

Both thresholds pass comfortably. Checkout-api's HPA scales smoothly from 6 replicas to 18, cluster-wide CPU holds around 52 percent, and the FinOps dashboard shows nothing unusual. By every number this test reports, the platform looks ready.

But all 500 virtual users originate from one pipeline agent, in one region, ramping smoothly. That's standard synthetic load, and it correctly tests CPU, memory, and HPA scaling — it just never creates the rapid, bursty, multi-origin scale-out that real holiday traffic will.

That bursty pattern is exactly the condition under which the scheduler, with no topology spread constraint since Lesson 4, is most likely to concentrate new pods onto whichever zone happens to have room in the moment. The test passed honestly — it simply was never scoped to ask this second question at all.
